pageIntro: What to check in results and how to move calculated doses into the tank without surprises.

sections.title: Quick start: from water to finished solution
sections.summary: Tab order and a short mixing workflow.

blocks.text: Set your farm and, when possible, link the recipe to a grow cycle — that makes it easier to repeat a good feeding after harvest.
Steps

items: Water: enter source analysis (sodium, chloride, and alkalinity when you have them; EC and pH if available). A saved farm profile fills in automatically.
Feed systems: pick a manufacturer step or your own system — target ppm and, if set, step EC and pH apply.
Fertilizers: select the products you feed with.
Magic wand: set tank volume, single tank or A/B layout, optional EC cap and ammonium share — you get up to five dose options.
Review the deviation table, EC estimate, and warnings. Save the recipe and optionally log feeding to the cycle journal.

blocks.text: The Solutions tab stores saved recipes: reload into a calculation, repeat in a new cycle, or duplicate.
Label compositions and trust levels — on the Data sources page.

sections.title: How doses are calculated
sections.summary: What comes from water, labels, and element targets.

blocks.text: You set element targets in ppm (mg/L) and a fertilizer list. The app finds the doses that bring the whole solution closest to target without crossing the limits you set. How deviations are weighed is described below.
Label composition becomes tank contribution: oxide values on the pack (P₂O₅, K₂O, etc.) convert to elemental share; dose in g/L or mL/L becomes ppm.
Source water

What is already in water is subtracted from the target. If water exceeds your target for an element, you get a warning and the target is adjusted. Alkalinity can include acid neutralization — then added nitrogen or phosphorus enters the calculation.
How deviations are weighed

Each element's deviation is taken as a percent of its target and squared: a 20% shortfall weighs four times as much as 10%. So the app prefers several small deviations to one large one. Deviations are then added up with weights.
Here T is the target, A the achieved value, w the element weight, and k the overshoot multiplier (it equals one for a shortfall).

items: N, P and K weigh 3; Ca, Mg and S weigh 2; micronutrients weigh 1.
Overshoot costs more than shortfall: 1.25 times for macros, twice for micros. Excess micronutrients turn toxic sooner, and nothing can be taken back out of a tank.

Elements without a target (boron and manganese from a micro mix when only iron is set, or sodium from a salt) cost nothing until they pass the top of their usual working range: B 0.5, Mn 1, Zn 0.5, Cu 0.1, Mo 0.05, Fe 2, Na and Cl 10 ppm. Above that level they are penalized.
The sum is divided by the total weight of targeted elements, so an extra element cannot dilute the score.

blocks.text: Overdose limits and other constraints

items: Each element has an upper overdose band vs target: NPK often up to +20%, Ca, Mg, and S up to +30%, micros up to +50%.
The macro limit is hard: the app never exceeds it. If the target cannot be reached without overshoot, you get a shortfall instead.

The micro limit is soft. It can be exceeded when the micronutrient comes as an impurity in a needed macro salt, or in a micro mix with a different element ratio. Above the limit the penalty grows faster and a yellow warning names the element. Example: the app will not cut P and K by 10% to avoid 0.01 ppm of copper from an NPK salt.
Doses round to 0.001 g or mL per liter of working solution. Limits are checked on the rounded doses.
You can set an EC cap, NH₄ share of total nitrogen, and a product dose cap when solubility limits apply. These limits are hard too.
Same-brand A+B pairs dose in the manufacturer ratio (usually 1:1).

blocks.text: EC estimate and other units
The EC estimate is guidance from composition. After mixing, still measure EC and pH with a meter. On the Elements tab you can view mmol/L and mg-eq/L — useful to compare with lab reports.
How far you can trust the result

The dose problem is solved exactly, without random search: for these weights and limits the program finds the best set of doses. The doses are then rounded to a 0.001 g/L step, and nearby rounding options are checked, so the result is practically as good as the exact solution. The same inputs always give the same doses.

items: Independent check: the same problem is solved separately by a Python program (the SciPy scientific library). On 12 reference recipes the result matches in 9, and in 3 ours is slightly better. On 60 random sets of 3–8 fertilizers our answer was never worse.

Comparison with Hydroodo on 12 recipes with the same products and targets: on the overall deviation score ours is better in all 12. Macro match is higher in 8 recipes and lower by at most 1 point in 3. In one, Hydroodo is closer on macros because it delivers copper at 262% of target against its own 150% limit; ours gives 163% with a warning.
A trade-off example: in a recipe where iron is the only micronutrient target, we hit the Fe target and keep Ca at 71% of target; Hydroodo gives Fe 90% and Ca 30%.
The wand is checked separately: shown ppm are always recomputed from the shown doses, macro limits hold, and a rerun gives the same result.

blocks.text: What the calculation does not know: label accuracy (check the product's trust level), precipitation and binding in the tank, element availability at your pH, and plant uptake. The app counts how much of each element you add, not how much will be taken up. The weights and limits above are sensible defaults, not a law: if your crop has other priorities, compare options in the deviation table.

The objective is a weighted sum of squared relative deviations; it is convex and the constraints are linear. Such a problem has no false local minima, so the minimum is found exactly: projected Newton on the dose bounds, with limits, NH₄ share and EC handled by an augmented Lagrangian (EC is linearized step by step).

Doses are then rounded to 0.001: the nearest grid nodes are enumerated, then single and paired dose steps. If a small dose (a micro mix) sits on a limit, it is pinned to neighboring nodes in turn and the other doses are re-solved. The reference for checks is SciPy (SLSQP with 24–64 random starts).
EC estimate uses an ionic-strength model (ion charge and interaction in solution).

sections.title: Magic wand
sections.summary: Up to five mix options and what match percent means.

blocks.text: The wand tries combinations from your selected fertilizers and solves doses for each. You see the best option and up to four alternates — five tabs maximum.

items: The mix must include a source for every macro that has a target.
Alternates often swap the main calcium, potassium, phosphorus, or magnesium product for another from your list.
When an A+B pair is in the mix, both parts dose in the manufacturer ratio (usually 1:1); other salts fill the rest.

The wand shows no dose below 0.01 g/L: such a line is either raised to 0.01 or removed, whichever lands closer to target. For micro mixes the floor is 0.001 g/L (1 mg/L), since they are dosed in milligrams.
A product that barely improves the solution is dropped: a shorter recipe is easier to mix.
Alternates with any macro more than 25% under or over target are discarded. If no option qualifies, the wand shows the closest one with a match of 74% at most.
Very similar product sets merge so duplicates do not clutter the list.
Shown ppm are always computed from the shown doses: there are no hidden additions.

blocks.text: Macro match percent is the average, over macros with a target, of 100 minus the absolute percent deviation. One hundred percent hits every macro exactly; ninety or higher is often workable — still read the deviation table and warnings.
Order of options: higher match percent first (as shown, to the whole number); at equal percent, fewer products; then the lower overall deviation score including micronutrients.

With several options, use Compare variants: rows are elements, columns are mixes. Green means under ten percent deviation, yellow ten to twenty, red twenty or more; + or − shows overshoot or undershoot. Pick the column that fits your priorities, then review that mix below.

For A+B pairs, part B is matched to part A in the manufacturer ratio (usually 1:1), then remaining target is closed with other fertilizers. Each fertilizer set is solved exactly, as in the main calculation. Doses below the floor are settled by choosing raise-to-floor or remove on the overall deviation score.

For each element with a non-zero target you see target ppm, achieved ppm including water, difference in ppm and percent. In tolerance means the result sits between allowed undershoot and overdose ceiling for that element.

Yellow warnings may note missing liquid density, an over-concentrated stock, or ammonium above your cap. Even with low match, the closest option still shows — check the table carefully before feeding.

The “Micronutrient above its overdose limit” warning refers to the soft limit: the element came with a product the mix needs, and lowering it would pull the rest further from target. If that element is critical for your crop (copper or boron, for example), remove or replace the source product.

sections.title: Water
sections.summary: Why your own analysis matters and what to watch in Na, Cl, alkalinity, and pH.

blocks.text: The same recipe on different water yields different tanks: well potassium and calcium reduce salt doses; sodium and chloride accumulate; bicarbonate alkalinity shifts pH and acid use.

items: Enter at least sodium, chloride, and alkalinity — they feed the target calculation.
Alkalinity can be bicarbonate (mg/L) or CaCO₃ equivalent — the calculator converts.
Water pH and EC on the card are for your records; measure finished solution pH after mixing.
Neutralizing alkalinity adds nitrogen (nitric acid) or phosphorus (phosphoric) — account for that in targets.

sections.title: Elements and salt composition
sections.summary: Reference and real elemental contribution from labels.

blocks.text: On the Elements tab: atomic weights, oxide-to-element conversion, and shares in selected products after label recalculation.
Even “pure” salts carry certificate impurities in practice (sodium in magnesium sulfate, chloride in calcium forms). Calculation uses declared percentages, not ideal stoichiometry.

sections.title: Feed systems and grow cycles
sections.summary: Feeding steps, crop linkage, repeating after harvest.

blocks.text: A feed system is your week or stage steps: target ppm, EC, and pH. The active step feeds the wand target. Linking to a grow cycle keeps the plan with the crop; a feeding log writes to the farm event journal.

items: After harvest, on Solutions you can repeat a recipe in a new cycle or copy the plan.
A recipe tied to a feeding journal entry deletes only with confirmation.
For yourself, keep recipe name, volume, doses, and measured EC and pH after mixing.

sections.title: Data sources and trust
sections.summary: Where label numbers come from and how much to rely on them.

blocks.text: Each catalog product lists a data source and trust level: high, medium, low, or not yet verified. That shows whether you rely on official labels, manufacturer tables, or community references.

How the calculation itself is checked, and what it does not account for, is described under “How doses are calculated”. The same ppm target can be built with different salt sets — compare achieved ppm, not only grams per liter.
Full source list and update dates
Mixing order (working solution)

items: Fill the tank about three quarters with clean water.
Add part A (calcium forms), mix well.
Add part B (sulfates, phosphates), mix again.
Add micros and chelates if not already in A/B.
Top up to full volume.
Adjust pH last and measure EC of the finished solution.

blocks.text: In concentrate, calcium with sulfates or phosphates precipitates (gypsum, calcium phosphate), so A and B dilute in water separately. Do not mix A and B concentrates directly — water first. With A/B in the calculator, calcium does not share a concentrate with sulfates and phosphates: follow tank hints.
Chelates and precision

items: Fe-EDTA usually holds iron to about pH 6.5; Fe-DTPA to about 7.5; Fe-EDDHA for more alkaline conditions.
Doses round to 0.001 g/mL per liter; on large tanks scale to total volume and weigh to your scale precision.
Follow SDS and concentrate storage rules.

blocks.text: Before feeding plants, measure EC and pH of the finished solution with calibrated meters and check against crop and growth stage.

items: Why do doses differ from Hydroodo? One target can be met with different doses, and the apps choose the trade-off differently. Hydroodo may sacrifice one element heavily (leaving Ca at 30% of target, for example) to hit the rest; we spread the deviation more evenly. Compare achieved ppm.

Why does the wand suggest a micro mix at 0.002 g/L? Micro mixes are concentrated and dosed in milligrams per liter. For a 100 L tank that is 0.2 g: weigh it on a jewelry scale or make a stock solution.
Why two label calculation modes? Canonical (element) mode suits modern databases; the other mode compares to legacy tables if you still use them.
Why does EC estimate differ from my meter? Temperature, organics, and impurities affect readings; measure after mixing.
What if liquid density is missing on the label? The app warns and assumes 1.00 g/mL; enter density on the product card for precise milliliters.
Does calculation work offline? Yes, after the catalog is on the device; saving a recipe to the farm needs network.
How many wand variants? At most five tabs: one primary and up to four alternates.
